newsitem.title: USA: Meyer urges caution on mixing US banking, commerce.
newsitem.headline: Meyer urges caution on mixing US banking, commerce.

text.p: Lawmakers should be cautious about permitting unrestricted mixing of banking and commercial businesses as part of a broad reform effort, Federal Reserve Governor Laurence Meyer said on Thursday.

Speaking to a conference on financial structure at the Jerome Levy Economics Institute of Bard College in Annandale-on-Hudson, N.Y., the Fed governor said that "in an uncertain world characterized by rapid change, caution is not a dirty word."
A text of his remarks was issued in Washington.

Meyer said that banking and commerce currently were "essentially separate activities" in the United States. "Thus, we need to think carefully about whether we want to go even further down the road of combining banking with nonfinancial activities," he said.

The arguments that are put forward for unrestricted mixing of banking and commerce were not convincing, Meyer said, and some, like the claim that more combination was needed to attract capital to banking, appeared "pretty silly."
U.S. banks have enjoyed five years of record profits and capital is flowing into the industry, he said.

Meyer said another reason for caution lay in the need to modify supervisory techniques. Regulators can handle the challenge of expanded financial activities by banks but it might be "a bridge too far" to also add commercial firms.
"Indeed, I believe that prudent public policy requires that, for this reason alone, we get financial activities right before tackling further combinations of banking and commerce," Meyer said.
He suggested banking reform today should focus on expanding permissible financial activities instead of moving toward mixing commerce and banking.
"The prohibitions against banking and securities and banking and insurance combinations have always, it seems to me, been difficult to support," Meyer said.
He did not totally rule out more mixing of banking and commerce but said it should be done carefully to maintain bank safety.
"Once we have mastered the art and science of supervising full service financial organizations, then perhaps we should consider further combining banking and commerce," Meyer said.
